title: Three Months on a Seville Roof Taught Him to Paint Exactly What Was There. It Cost Him His Job Sixteen Years Later.
standfirst: In 1870 a young Thomas Eakins spent three months on a Seville rooftop trying to paint an ordinary street in full, shifting sun. The same refusal to paint around a hard truth ended his career at the Pennsylvania Academy sixteen years later — and kept this canvas out of a museum for a hundred and fifty-three years.

sections.heading: He Called It "The Most Difficult Kind of a Picture"
sections.body: Eakins was newly out of Jean-Léon Gérôme's Paris atelier when he hauled an easel onto the roof of his Seville hotel and began the first large canvas he had ever attempted outside a studio. The subject was ordinary — a street, some figures, full sun — and that was exactly the problem. Paris had trained his eye on steady, silvery, north-facing studio light; Seville's, according to the curator Kathleen A. Foster, "is very strong, it's changing quickly, and Eakins had a terrible time." He later described the kind of picture he had set himself, a figure subject in direct outdoor light, as the most difficult kind of a picture there is, and kept at it anyway, hiring a family of itinerant street musicians, the Requeñas, to hold their places through sitting after sitting. The canvas that resulted, more than five feet tall, is filed under Impressionism in the record behind this page. WikiArt's own page for it — the record this page draws from — calls it Realism instead, the far less surprising label for a painter trained by Gérôme and Léon Bonnat who spent his career arguing against exactly what Monet's generation was doing with light.

sections.heading: He Had Chased One Painting Across Spain to Get There
sections.body: On 29 November 1869, straight off the train from Paris, Eakins went to the Prado before he did anything else. Diego Velázquez's Las Hilanderas stopped him the way nothing in Paris had: he judged it, by his own account, the most beautiful painting he had ever seen, and filled a pocket notebook with technical notes on how Velázquez had built it — thin, transparent glazes over a solidly painted underlayer, the same method he decided had made Rembrandt's late portraits work too. Two teachers had sent him to Spain knowing roughly what he would find: Gérôme, under whom he had trained in figure drawing since 1866, and Bonnat, who had painted in Spain himself and pushed him toward the detour. He stayed in Madrid only long enough to copy what he could from Velázquez and Ribera, then went on to Seville for what became six months.

sections.heading: The Easy Portrait and the Impossible One Came From the Same Family
sections.body: The Requeñas gave Eakins two very different jobs that winter. The daughter, seven-year-old Carmelita, sat for a loose, quick oil sketch, twenty-one by seventeen inches, done in a sitting or two. The street scene asked for the whole family, posed and held outdoors for more than three months, in a composition built on the scale of something meant to be exhibited rather than practiced. The two canvases then took wildly different paths into public view. Carmelita reached the Metropolitan Museum in 1978, in the bequest of Mary Cushing Fosburgh. The street scene stayed in private hands, sold on from one collection to the next without ever entering a museum, until the Wolf family gave it to the Met in 2023 — a hundred and seven years after Eakins himself had died, and a hundred and fifty-three after he painted it.

sections.heading: Back in Philadelphia, the Same Refusal to Soften Things Had a Cost
sections.body: Eakins carried the habit he'd formed on that roof — insisting on exactly what was in front of him — into the classroom. As director of the Pennsylvania Academy's school from 1882, he taught anatomy from actual dissections and ran nude-model sessions in mixed classes, against prevailing custom. In January 1886 he had a male model remove his loincloth during an anatomy demonstration in front of a mixed class. The Academy's director of education asked for his resignation on 8 February; Eakins sent a one-sentence reply the next day, and the board accepted it on 13 February. Fifty-five of his male students signed a petition for his reinstatement that went nowhere, then founded a school around him instead, the Art Students' League of Philadelphia, where he taught unpaid until 1893.

sections.heading: The Academy Had Already Flinched Once Before
sections.body: Ten years earlier, the same unwillingness to look away had cost him a different stage. The Gross Clinic, his 1875 portrait of the surgeon Samuel Gross operating in front of students with blood visible on his hand, was turned down by the fine-arts jury of the 1876 Centennial Exhibition as too graphic. It hung instead in the exhibition's medical section, among displays about Philadelphia's hospitals, drawing attention as a curiosity of medicine rather than as a painting. The jury's objection in 1876 and the Academy's complaint in 1886 were, underneath the different language, the same complaint: that Eakins painted what was actually there, including the parts a polite audience would rather not have had shown to it.

sections.heading: He Sold Fewer Than Thirty Paintings Before the Verdict Changed
sections.body: Eakins had one solo exhibition in his lifetime and sold fewer than thirty paintings total. He kept teaching, unpaid, through the 1890s, and died in 1916 largely outside the canon he is now filed under as one of its anchors. The reversal took Lloyd Goodrich's 1933 study to get moving, and it has not really stopped since: the Gross Clinic now hangs as one of American art's acknowledged major works, and the Academy that forced Eakins out eventually built part of its reputation on having trained him. The street scene he fought the Seville sun over for three months took longer than either to catch up. Hidden in private houses for a century and a half, it only joined a public collection in 2023 — the same unflinching accuracy that once got its painter fired now simply called connoisseurship.
